newsitem.title: MEXICO: Emerging markets struggle to protect investors.
newsitem.headline: Emerging markets struggle to protect investors.

text.p: Stock markets in emerging markets, struggling to expand while at the same time protect investors, are finding that balance is not always easy to strike, stock market regulators said on Wednesday.

Placing too many regulations on companies wanting to list on an exchange can push those companies away, but rampant abuses such as insider trading can turn off investors, executives from emerging markets said at a conference on global stock markets.

"Regulations are needed for a well-organized market, but you must try to establish a balance between the needs of companies and investors," Edgar I. Jelonche, chief executive officer of the Bolsa de Comercio de Buenos Aires, said.
He, as well as other executives, pointed to the need to increase disclosure.

"Disclosure is essential. If you don't establish rules for market disclosure to prevent insider trading, you cannot organize a market," Jelonche told attendees at the conference of the International Federation of Stock Exchanges.
Paul C.Y. Huang, director of research for the Taiwan Stock Exchange, noted that his stock market, like others, has undertaken efforts to educate investors about insider trading.
"It (insider trading) is not as prevalent as people think," he said. "If insider trading were typical, investors would stop trading."

Ku Rahman Ku Sulaiman, senior vice-president of the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange, said the exchange has put in place rules to stop company directors from trading within certain time limits of important releases of data. But he also said that over-regulation of markets could be counter-productive.
"Regulation is necessary but over-regulation is counter- productive to countries trying to develop their emerging markets," he said.

Edgar Cheng, chairman of the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong, noted that in emerging markets neither investors nor issuers of securities may be aware of their rights. Too much disclosure may deter issuers, which could be a problem for exchanges trying to attract more companies, he added.
Still, the executives pointed out that having effective regulations are a permanent concern and the rules should aim to promote transparency.
However, each country must seek to find the best solutions for each distinct market.
"It seems to me that regulatory models cannot simply be transplanted from one country to another," said Buenos Aires' Jelonche.
The Taiwan market has instituted a number of measures, including setting up a protection fund for investors, said Huang.
